newsitem.title: USA: American 'ready' to reach deal with its pilots.
newsitem.headline: American 'ready' to reach deal with its pilots.

text.p: With an emergency labour board ending five days of critical contract hearings between American Airlines and its pilots, the chairman of American said on Wednesday "it's time to make a deal."

But Robert Crandall told reporters that a "deal" on general wages and the wages of pilots who will fly the new small regional jets American intends to buy had to enable the number two U.S. airline to remain competitive.
A spokesman for the Allied Pilots Association, Wally Pitts, agreed separately that the dispute had gone on too long and that "It's time to close these negotiations."
Neither side indicated, however, that they had changed the positions that led to the Feb. 4 stalemate and pilot's strike.
Minutes after that strike began, President Clinton created the three-member Presidential Emergency Board (PEB), sending the pilots back to work.

Under the law, the pilots cannot strike for the 30 days while the board meets to take testimony and tries to fashion a settlement agreeable to both sides and then for another 30 days while the two sides consider the recommendations.
The board is to submit its proposals to the two sides and Clinton by March 17, with the second 30 days starting then.

Crandall said American had agreed to a contract last year, which was later rejected by the pilots, and again to one offered by mediators the night before the strike, also rejected. He said, "We are ready to make a deal now."
He added that "we are very hopeful that the PEB will come forward with a recommendation that we can accept, and we very much hope that the union will accept it as well."
Pitts said the board of the APA, which represents 9,300 American pilots, had scheduled a meeting on March 21, four days after it receives the PEB's recommendations.
If the union strikes again, Congress could step in and require binding arbitration, but Crandall, asked about this, said "I have no idea whether Congress will intervene."
The APA had opposed the creation of the PEB and is opposed to Congressional action, preferring to allow the pilots to work it out, using labour's weapon of the strike.
A Transportation Department estimate given Clinton, on which he in part based his decision to create the PEB, said an American strike would cost the economy $200 million a day.

The dispute centres on two main issues. One is pay. The APA wants an increase of 11 percent to cover the past three years when it got no pay increase and the next four years. American has offered 6.5 percent.

The other is who will pilot the new, small jets for American's commuter carrier, American Eagle. The APA wants its members, who average $120,000 a year, to be in the cockpit, but American wants the planes to be flown by Eagle pilots, who belong to another union and earn far less.
American has said it needed lower-paid pilots to fly the new small jets so American Eagle could be competitive with the low-cost commuter lines operated by other major carriers.
